justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I would have assessed as the prevailing level of the S&P 500 around the 505–506 range at the time of the forecast. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price, applying only a small positive drift consistent with the historical average daily return of equities, which is statistically near zero over any single session. For the one-week horizon, I extended that drift slightly further, acknowledging that equity markets have a slight positive bias over short periods but that mean reversion and noise dominate. For the one-month horizon, the point estimate of 512 reflects an annualized return assumption of roughly 8–10%, prorated to one month, which translates to perhaps a 1–1.5% expected gain from the starting level. These are all fairly conservative assumptions grounded in long-run equity market behavior rather than any specific near-term catalyst.

The confidence interval widths are driven primarily by historical realized volatility. The S&P 500 has an annualized volatility of roughly 15–18%, which translates to daily volatility of about 1% and weekly volatility of around 2–2.5%. At one month, that widens to roughly 4–5%. My 90% confidence intervals are somewhat tighter than a pure statistical model would suggest for the one-month horizon, reflecting an implicit assumption that the near-term macro environment was not in an extreme stress regime at the time of the forecast. The one-day interval of roughly plus or minus 10 points around 506 is consistent with typical daily ranges, while the one-month interval of roughly plus or minus 34 points captures a substantial portion of plausible outcomes under normal conditions.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharp rise in unemployment claims, a sudden credit event, or a geopolitical shock — could produce a drawdown of 5–10% or more within a month, easily breaching the lower bound. Federal Reserve communication that surprises markets with a more hawkish stance than priced in could similarly trigger a rapid repricing. On the upside, a significant positive surprise in corporate earnings, a favorable inflation print that accelerates rate cut expectations, or a resolution of geopolitical tensions could push the index above the upper bound. Tail risks, by definition, are not well-captured in 90% intervals, and in equity markets, left-tail events tend to be more severe and faster-moving than right-tail rallies, which introduces an asymmetry worth bearing in mind.
